Consult Summary:
- 43-year-old male developed acute shortness of breath, chest tightness, lip tingling, and blotchy rash within 15 min of a wasp sting; advised to take an antihistamine and call an ambulance for suspected early anaphylaxis.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Breathing difficulty after a wasp sting.
- Timeline
  • ~15 min prior to call: stung by a wasp while gardening → ran indoors.  
  • Since then: shallow breathing and chest tightness.  
- Associated symptoms: Tingling sensation in lips; blotchy skin rash.  
- Denies: Throat closing sensation; prior similar reactions.  
- No medications taken yet today.
- Pertinent negatives: No known swelling of lips/throat; no mention of wheeze heard.

Past Medical History:
- Eczema (no current flare discussed).
- Penicillin allergy (drug allergy).
- Aerosinusitis when flying (uses antihistamines PRN).
- No other significant medical or surgical history volunteered.

Medications:
- Antihistamine (kept at home for flying; dose/route/frequency not documented).
- No regular daily medications reported.
Allergies:
- Penicillin → allergic reaction (details not provided).

Social History:
- Lives with wife; wife present and able to assist.
- Gardening at home at time of incident.
- Tobacco/alcohol/substance use: not discussed.
- Occupation and other lifestyle factors: not discussed.

Family History:
- Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded (remote video consultation).
- General/skin: Patient reports blotchy rash.
- HEENT: Tingling lips; patient denies throat swelling.
- Respiratory: Subjective shallow breathing and chest tightness (no objective auscultation possible).
- Cardiovascular/Abd/Neuro: Not assessed.
- Overall: Remote assessment—no direct examination possible.

Investigations:
- None obtained during consultation.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
- Suspected early anaphylaxis (or rapidly evolving systemic allergic reaction) secondary to wasp sting, given acute respiratory and cutaneous symptoms.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Anaphylaxis secondary to wasp sting  
   • Supporting: Immediate onset, respiratory difficulty, cutaneous rash, lip tingling; clinician urgency.  
   • Opposing: No overt lip/throat swelling or hemodynamic compromise documented.
2. Systemic allergic urticaria (without full anaphylaxis)  
   • Supporting: Rash and tingling without definitive airway compromise.  
   • Opposing: Respiratory symptoms raise concern for progression to anaphylaxis.

Issue 1 – Possible Anaphylaxis:
- Assessment: Acute respiratory and cutaneous manifestations shortly after wasp sting; high risk for progression.
- Plan:
  • Instructed patient’s wife to call emergency medical services (ambulance) immediately.  
  • Advised patient to take an oral antihistamine while awaiting EMS.  
  • Urgent transport to Emergency Department for evaluation, monitoring, and potential epinephrine and airway management.  
  • Provided rationale and emphasized time sensitivity.

Issue 2 – Drug Allergy (Penicillin):
- Assessment: Known allergy; relevance for future prescribing.
- Plan:
  • Document clearly in records; ensure hospital staff aware.

Issue 3 – Chronic Skin Condition (Eczema):
- Assessment: Stable; not contributory to current emergency.
- Plan:
  • No action today; continue existing self-care.

General plan items:
- Encourage patient to obtain an epinephrine auto-injector after acute episode and arrange follow-up with allergy specialist for venom immunotherapy discussion. (Education to be reinforced during hospital or GP follow-up.)

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: No vitals, no full medication reconciliation, no social/family history on smoking/alcohol; not obtainable in emergent context.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; limited past history explored due to urgency.
